bib.title: Evaluating the Goal-Directedness of Large Language Models

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: Extraction was clean. All 41 pages (134,998 chars) were read. Pages 1-9 (body) were read in full. The references were skimmed for origins. Appendices A-E were read in full. Appendix F (example transcripts, p.17 onward) was skimmed: I read the start and treated it as raw logs. I viewed Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 as an image (p.6).

SOURCE: "Evaluating the Goal-Directedness of Large Language Models". First author Tom Everitt (Google DeepMind), co-first author Cristina Garbacea (University of Chicago). Other authors: Alexis Bellot, Jonathan Richens, Rohin Shah (Google DeepMind), Henry Papadatos and Simeon Campos (SaferAI). arXiv 2504.11844v1, 16 Apr 2025. No venue is stated, so treat it as a preprint. The text has an ICML-style Impact Statement. Code: github.com/Crista23/goal_directedness_llms.

CORE CLAIM: Goal-directedness is the propensity to use the capabilities you have. It is not the same as task performance. The paper defines it as GD = (E[R_π] − E[R_π0]) / (max E[R_π*c] − E[R_π0]). R_π0 is a uniformly random baseline policy. The max term is the return you would get with full use of the capabilities measured on isolated subtasks. GD = 1 is full use and GD = 0 is random.

In the authors' words: "Our approach to measuring goal-directedness is to compare the agent's actual performance with the performance that could have been achieved with full use of its capabilities." (p.3)

HEADLINE FINDINGS
The text gives almost no numeric GD values; they sit in figures. I read these only from the bar charts, so they are approximate and I do not quote them as numbers.
1. Setup for all results: Blocksworld, 8 models, 30 seeds per task and subtask, with 3, 4 and 5 blocks. Models: gemini-1.5-flash, gemini-1.5-pro, gemini-2.0-flash, gpt-3.5-turbo-0125, gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09, gpt-4o-2024-11-20, claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219, claude-3-5-haiku-20241022. Queried March and April 2025 through LangChain. Metric: GD from Monte Carlo simulation, 10000 simulations per task and setting, with 95% bootstrap CIs (clustered by block count). Runs that did not finish in about 100 steps were excluded. Thinking models were excluded because they hallucinated environment responses.
2. Most models are not fully goal-directed. The closest are Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Gemini 2.0 Flash, and even they fall "somewhat short" on Information Gathering and Combined, though the paper says "we can't say with certainty". Reading Fig. 3 by eye, gpt-3.5 is about 0.48 on Information Gathering.
3. Models take fewer measurements when height estimation is a step in a larger task than when it is the only task. The paper says this holds "without exception" (Fig. 4). By eye, the Height Estimation bars are about 3.5 to 7 measurements per block, and the composite-task bars are about 1.2 to 3. The paper does not state these numbers.
4. Goal-directedness differs from performance. On Plan and Execute, no model is perfect, yet Gemini 2.0 Flash and Claude 3.7 Sonnet are near full GD. GPT-4 and GPT-4o execute near-perfectly in isolation but are no better than the others on the composite task, so they score lower on GD.
5. Model ordering is roughly the same across the four composite tasks. It also matches two alternative measures: rebuilding a falling tower (15 blocks) and the median number of measurements in Height Estimation. The exceptions are the Gemini models on the tower task and Gemini 1.5 Flash on measurements.
6. Prompting: a motivating prompt ("really go for it") raises performance and a demotivating one ("your answer doesn't matter, so why bother") lowers it. The test was Gemini 2.0 Flash on Information Gathering only (Fig. 9). Motivating the model is "still far from" the full-capability level.
7. Context-length control (App. E): the models were stepped through the subtasks in one context. Only the Gemini models were tested. Performance was generally better than on the composite task, so context length does not explain the drop. Gemini 1.5 Flash is an exception.

QUOTES
- "Rather, it is the (un)willingness to employ a capability that measures goal-directedness" (p.2)
- "Without exception, models take significantly fewer measurements in the latter case" (p.5)

LIMITS (as conceded by the authors, plus what the paper does not show)
- It uses one synthetic environment, Blocksworld. The authors say ideal coverage would be "100s of tasks across 10s of domains", and they leave that to future work.
- Capability is inferred from isolated subtasks. This assumes the model knows how to compose them, and that small subtasks need less goal-directedness than long ones. The authors admit a larger task could be more motivating, or give the model time to fix mistakes.
- It tests only the goal given in the prompt. It does not test intrinsic goals or fine-tuned objectives such as brevity or helpfulness, which could conflict with the task.
- Several models reach full GD on Cognitive Effort yet fall short elsewhere, so a full score on one decomposition does not prove full goal-directedness.
- It covers non-scaffolded models only, with no tree-of-thought or subgoal decomposition. There is no fine-tuning study, and no reasoning or thinking models.
- The sensitivity analysis covers a single model and a single task.
- There are no p-values for the cross-task consistency. The ordering is shown by eye, and the paper says only "roughly the same".
- The paper is from early 2025, and the models are now dated.
- The paper is about agents' propensity to use their capabilities. It is not about how to grade agent trajectories or outcomes.

BUILDS ON
- Capability-versus-propensity framing: MacDermott et al. 2024 (Measuring goal-directedness), Shimi et al. 2021 and Orseau et al. 2018. The paper says these equate goal-directedness with performance.
- Human tests: progress ratio tasks (Chen et al. 2022) and the anagram persistence test (Gignac & Wong 2020).
- Related AI work: Bellos et al. 2024 on goal-oriented reasoning, and Valmeekam et al. 2024 (PlanBench).
- Hong et al. 2023 on goal-directed dialogue, and Arike et al. 2024 (LessWrong).
- Chain-of-thought (Wei et al. 2022), the long-context papers (Liu et al. 2024, "Lost in the middle"), and Li et al. 2023 for the emotional-stimuli prompts.

BEST-FIT NOTE SECTION: "Evaluate the components, then the whole" fits best. The paper's method is to score subtasks in isolation, then compare the composite-task result against what those subtask scores predict. The gap between the two is the finding. The note's current section only says to grade each box (router, skills) separately so you can locate a failure. It lacks the idea that component scores can predict the composite score, and that the shortfall is a separate failure mode: the agent has the capability but under-uses it, for example by taking fewer measurements inside a bigger task. "Outcome and trajectory" fits less well. The paper does not grade trajectories, although the measurement-count result is a behavioural signal.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Fig. 4 (p.6), "Measurements per block", comparing standalone Height Estimation with the same step inside Information Gathering and Combined, for all 8 models. It shows the capability-versus-use gap at a glance. Fig. 1 (p.1) is the conceptual version, but I did not view it.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Equation symbols in the extraction are garbled (the GD formula spacing). Numbers read from figures are approximate, and the paper's text does not state them.
